title: Agreement in sentences
keyIdea: A verb must agree with its subject, and a pronoun must agree with its antecedent. Find the head noun of the subject and cross out any phrase after it: the box of crayons is, because one box. One of, each, every and everyone are singular. With neither … nor, the verb matches the nearer subject. In there is or there are, the subject comes after the verb. A pronoun matches the noun it stands for, even in the sentence before: the bikes were muddy, so Dad washed them.
familyTip: Read a sentence from a book with a long subject, such as 'The bag of apples is heavy.' Ask: what is the one word the sentence is about? Cover the extra phrase with a finger and read it again. Do the same with a pronoun: point back to the word it stands for.

visual.caption: Singular or plural subject? Drag each subject, or tap it and then a box.

bins: More than one: are, have, run

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap the head noun and cross out the phrase, drag the verb that agrees, use each and neither … nor, link pronouns to antecedents, fix a note.

kid: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. The verb must agree with it. One thing takes is, was, has, or a verb with s. More than one takes are, were, have, or no s.
A long subject can trick you. In 'The box of crayons is on the shelf', the main word is box. Of crayons just adds detail. Cover it up: the box is. That main word is called the head noun.
Some words are always one. Each, every, everyone and one of are singular: one of my friends has a dog. Two things joined by and make more than one: Sam and Ali catch the bus.

With neither … nor, look at the subject nearer the verb: neither the cat nor the dogs are hungry. In 'there are', the subject comes after the verb: there are two pens. A pronoun stands for a noun said earlier. That noun is its antecedent. They must match too. The tree dropped its leaves. The bikes were muddy, so Dad washed them.
adult: Ages 8 to 10. Agreement covers two links in a sentence: subject and verb (the box is, the boxes are) and pronoun and antecedent (the tree … its, the girls … their). US Common Core lists both under L.3.1f; in England, the Year 3–4 programme of study asks for Standard English verb forms and pronouns used for clarity across sentences.

The key skill is finding the head noun of the subject. Phrases after it, such as of crayons, in the park, as well as my coat, do not change the verb. One of, each and every take a singular verb. Compound subjects with and are plural. With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. In there is/there are, the subject follows the verb.

The lab has five tasks. Learners tap the head noun in six sentences and watch the phrase get crossed out, drag the right verb into seven gaps, apply the each, every, and, and neither … nor rules, drag pronouns that match their antecedents (with a line drawn back, including across sentences), and fix a note with three errors.

Common mistakes. The most frequent slip is attraction: matching the verb to the nearest noun (the box of crayons are, one of my friends have). Children also write there is two pens, treat each as plural, and use it for a plural antecedent. Note that collective nouns (the team is or are) and singular they (each pupil … their) are both accepted in British English and current style guides, so they are not marked wrong here.

practice.prompt: The bag of apples ___ heavy. Which verb fits?
practice.hint: Cover 'of apples'. What is the main word of the subject?
practice.explain: The head noun is bag, one bag, so the verb is is: the bag of apples is heavy.

practice.prompt: A pupil writes {n} sentences that start 'One of the ...', like 'One of the cats sleeps.' How many of these sentences need a singular verb?
practice.hint: What does 'one of' always mean, however many cats there are?
practice.explain: One of always means one, so every one of the {n} sentences takes a singular verb: one of the cats sleeps.

practice.prompt: Neither the dog nor the cats ___ inside.
practice.hint: Which subject is nearer the verb?
practice.explain: With neither … nor, the verb matches the nearer subject. Cats is plural, so are.

practice.prompt: A note has {v} verbs and {p} pronouns. You check that each one agrees with its subject or antecedent. How many checks do you make?
practice.hint: Every verb needs one check and every pronoun needs one check.
practice.explain: One check for each verb and each pronoun: {v} + {p} = {=v+p} checks.

practice.hint: Who is the antecedent, and how many are there?
practice.explain: The antecedent is the girls, more than one, so the pronoun is their.

pool.prompt: The children in the park ___ loud.
pool.hint: Cover 'in the park'. Is the head noun one or more than one?
pool.explain: The head noun is children, which is plural, so are.

pool.prompt: Each of the boys ___ a lunchbox.
pool.explain: Each means every single one, so it is singular: each of the boys has a lunchbox.

pool.prompt: There ___ two pens on the desk.
pool.hint: In 'there is/are', where is the subject?
pool.explain: The subject, two pens, comes after the verb. Two pens is plural, so there are.

pool.prompt: The box of pens fell. ___ lid came off.
pool.hint: Whose lid is it: the box's or the pens'?
pool.explain: The lid belongs to the box, one thing, so its lid. Pens is only inside 'of pens'.

pool.prompt: Which sentence has an agreement error?
choices: The key to the doors are lost.
The key to the doors is lost.
The keys to the door are lost.
pool.hint: Find the head noun in each subject.
pool.explain: The head noun is key, one key, so it should be is. 'Doors' tricks you because it sits next to the verb.

pool.prompt: The bikes were muddy. Dad washed ___.
pool.hint: Look back at the sentence before. What did Dad wash?
pool.explain: Them points back to the bikes in the sentence before. More than one bike, so them.

pool.hint: Two names joined by and: one or more than one?
pool.explain: Two people joined by and make a plural subject, so walk, with no s.

pool.prompt: In a story, {n} sentences use 'everyone' as the subject. How many of them need a singular verb like 'is' or 'has'?
pool.explain: Everyone is singular, so all {n} sentences need a singular verb: everyone is here.

pool.prompt: A pupil writes 'One of my friends have a dog.' What is the slip?
pool.hint: What is the subject really about: one or many?
pool.explain: The subject is one, so one of my friends has a dog. The verb was matched to the nearest noun, friends.

pool.prompt: A worksheet has {a} subjects joined by 'and', like 'Sam and Ali', and {e} subjects that start with 'Each', like 'Each of the boys'. How many of these subjects take a plural verb?
pool.hint: Which kind is plural: two things joined by and, or each?
pool.explain: Subjects joined by and are plural, so {a} take a plural verb. The {e} 'each' subjects are singular.

pool.prompt: Either the dogs or the cat ___ the bowl.
pool.hint: Which subject is nearer the verb?
pool.explain: With either … or, match the nearer subject. The cat is singular, so licks.
